lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Five Elements of Taste
lessons.0.slides.1.content: The interaction between food and wine is built on five taste elements: sweet, acid, bitter, salty, and umami. These elements influence one another: acidity can cut through fattiness, sweetness can temper heat, and tannins soften when they bind to protein. Understanding these fundamentals is the foundation of all high-level pairing. Successful pairing is not 'great wine + great food' — it is 'complementary or contrasting elements'.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🍷 Six Core Pairing Principles
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Complement: a rich Meursault with a cream sauce
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Contrast: high-acid Chablis with fatty foie gras
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Weight matching: light Volnay with poultry, full Pommard with red meat
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Flavour echo: earthy NSG with truffle or wild mushrooms
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Textural harmony: silky Chambolle with delicate fish
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: Regional echo: Burgundy wine with Burgundian cuisine (local tradition)
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Complementary vs Contrasting Pairing
lessons.0.slides.4.title: The Pivotal Role of Acidity
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Acidity is central to food and wine pairing. High-acid wines (Chablis, Puligny-Montrachet) can cut through fat, cleanse the palate, and stimulate the appetite. This is why oysters with Chablis is a classic: the marine salinity of the oyster and Chablis's high-acid minerality balance perfectly. Conversely, a low-acid wine with a fatty dish feels heavy. Remember: the richer the dish, the higher the acidity of the wine should be.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🔬 History of Flavour Science and Food and Wine Pairing Research
lessons.0.slides.6.title: ⚠️ Common Pairing Mistakes
lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: High-tannin wine with fish: tannins + fishiness = metallic bitterness
lessons.0.slides.6.points.1: High-acid wine with vinegar: acid + acid = overly sharp
lessons.0.slides.6.points.2: Sweet dish with a dry wine: dish is sweeter than wine, wine tastes bitter
lessons.0.slides.6.points.3: Spicy dish with a tannic red: heat + tannins = adding fuel to the fire
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: Delicate wine with a strong-flavoured dish: wine is overwhelmed by the food
lessons.0.slides.6.points.5: Ignoring the sauce: the sauce is often more important than the main ingredient
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 💡 Professional Pairing Tips
lessons.0.slides.7.points.0: Analyse the dish first: main ingredient, cooking method, sauce, garnishes
lessons.0.slides.7.points.1: Identify the dominant flavour: is it butter, spice, or pan juices?
lessons.0.slides.7.points.2: Define the wine's role: complement, contrast, or cleanse the palate?
lessons.0.slides.7.points.3: Consider the sequence: light to rich, white to red
lessons.0.slides.7.points.4: Temperature matters: white wine too cold masks flavour; red too warm emphasises alcohol
lessons.0.slides.7.points.5: Experiment and record: there are no absolute rules; build experience

lessons.1.slides.0.description: Perfect combinations passed down over a century
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Local Food with Local Wine
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Burgundy is not only a wine region — it is a gastronomic paradise. Local traditional cuisine evolved in step with the wine: Coq au Vin (chicken braised in red wine) with Gevrey, Escargots (snails) with Chablis, Bœuf Bourguignon (beef braised in red wine) with Pommard. These century-old pairings prove the wisdom of regional matching.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🇫🇷 Classic Burgundy Dish Pairings
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: Oysters (Huîtres) + Chablis Grand Cru: mineral and marine in perfect dialogue
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: Burgundy snails (Escargots) + Chablis or Meursault: garlic-butter needs acidity
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Coq au Vin + Gevrey-Chambertin: cook with the same wine you serve
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Bœuf Bourguignon + Pommard or NSG: powerful tannins match the braised beef
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Bresse chicken (white meat) + Volnay or Chambolle: delicacy matches delicacy
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Époisses cheese + Marc de Bourgogne or sweet white wine
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Classic White Wine Pairings
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Red Wine and Meat: The Logic
lessons.1.slides.4.content: The elegant tannins of Burgundy reds suit many meats, but cooking method matters: roasting (high heat) suits tannin-rich Pommard and NSG; braising (low heat) suits elegant Volnay and Chambolle; pan-searing (medium heat) suits Vosne and Morey. Poultry (duck, goose) suits Burgundy's refined style better than beef or lamb.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🍽️ Evolution of Classic French Food and Wine Pairings (Middle Ages→2026)
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🥩 Red Wine and Meat Guide
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Game (venison, wild boar) + Gevrey GC, Chambertin: powerful meets wild
lessons.1.slides.6.points.1: Duck breast + Vosne-Romanée: fat cut by tannins and acidity
lessons.1.slides.6.points.2: Lamb + Pommard, Volnay: the umami of lamb with the wine's fruit
lessons.1.slides.6.points.3: Beef fillet + Chambolle, Volnay: tender meat with an elegant wine
lessons.1.slides.6.points.4: Ribeye + Gevrey, NSG: marbling matched by powerful tannins
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 🧀 The Art of Cheese Pairing
lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: Soft cheeses (Brie, Camembert) + young red or Meursault
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Washed-rind cheeses (Époisses) + sweet white wine or Marc
lessons.1.slides.7.points.4: Blue cheese (Roquefort) + Sauternes (not Burgundy, but classic)
lessons.1.slides.7.points.5: Principle: regional match, weight match, avoid overpowering the wine

lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 19 min
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Challenges and Opportunities of Asian Cuisine
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Asian cuisine is a challenge for wine pairing: complex spices, heat, sweet-savoury balance, umami. Yet Burgundy's high acidity and minerality work surprisingly well: Chablis with sushi is already a classic; Meursault with Cantonese seafood; a light red with Peking duck. The key is to avoid overly spicy or sweet dishes and to choose the refined route.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🍣 Japanese Cuisine Pairings
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Sushi, sashimi + Chablis Grand Cru: mineral meets marine umami
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Tempura (fried) + Puligny-Montrachet: high acid cuts the grease
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Grilled eel (kabayaki) + Volnay, young Gevrey: sweet-savoury glaze with fruit
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Wagyu + Chambolle, Vosne: fat marbling with silky tannins
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Kaiseki + a flight of Burgundy (white → light red → full red)
lessons.2.slides.2.points.5: Caution: avoid too much wasabi — it overwhelms the wine
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Chinese Cuisine Pairing Strategy
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Southeast Asian and Indian Cuisine
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Southeast Asian cuisine (Thai, Vietnamese) with its complex sweet-sour-hot balance is a major challenge for Burgundy. Vietnamese phở's clean broth works with Chablis; Thai seafood with Puligny; but curries, laksa, and other rich, spice-heavy dishes overwhelm the wine. The same applies to Indian cuisine: heavily spiced dishes like Tikka Masala are not suited to delicate Burgundy — choose New World wines or beer instead.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🌏 Global Food and Wine Pairing Trends and the Evolution of East-West Fusion (1980→2026)

lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Oyster omelette (蚵仔煎) + Chablis: seafood umami with mineral
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Three-cup chicken (not spicy) + Gevrey village: soy-sweetness with fruit
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Steamed grouper + Meursault: delicate fish with full-bodied white
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Braised pork rice + light red (challenging): fatty pork needs acidity
lessons.2.slides.6.points.4: Popcorn chicken (fried) + Puligny: frying needs high acid
lessons.2.slides.6.points.5: Bubble tea: no match! Too sweet
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 💡 Asian Cuisine Pairing Tips
lessons.2.slides.7.points.0: Choose the refined route: high-end Japanese and Cantonese are easier than bold Sichuan
lessons.2.slides.7.points.1: White wine first: Burgundy whites' high acidity suits Asian seafood better
lessons.2.slides.7.points.2: Avoid extremes: very spicy, very sweet, very salty don't suit delicate wine
lessons.2.slides.7.points.3: Sauce is key: steamed > red-braised > mala spicy
lessons.2.slides.7.points.4: Creative experiment: Peking duck with Chambolle (fat with silky tannins)
lessons.2.slides.7.points.5: Cultural fusion: Michelin-starred Chinese restaurants have already proven it works

lessons.3.slides.1.title: The Sommelier's Role and Challenges
lessons.3.slides.1.content: The Chef Sommelier of a three-Michelin-star restaurant is not just a wine selector — they are an experience designer. They must: understand the chef's creative vision, balance the guest's budget and expectations, orchestrate the rhythm of the complete wine and food programme (from light to rich), handle special dietary requirements, and tell the story of each wine. An 8–12 course tasting menu needs wines that build in layers, creating a crescendo.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: ⭐ Top Restaurant Pairing Case Studies
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Maison Lameloise (Burgundy, 3 stars): full Burgundy wine list, local ingredients
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Le Bernardin (New York): seafood specialist, predominantly Chablis and white Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Eleven Madison Park: innovative American, Burgundy at the heart of the list
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: The French Laundry: classic French, DRC and top-tier Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Restaurant Guy Savoy (Paris): traditional French cuisine with traditional Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Quintessence (Tokyo): French-Japanese fusion — Burgundy is a perfect fit
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Tasting Menu Pairing Strategy
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Wine List Design Philosophy
lessons.3.slides.4.content: Top restaurant wine list design considerations: depth (multiple producers per village) vs breadth (global regions), price tiers (entry-level to luxury), vintage selection (drinking windows), and narrative (estate backgrounds). Burgundy-specialist restaurants like Maison Lameloise hold thousands of Burgundy labels, from village to DRC; comprehensive restaurants put Burgundy at 30–50%, balanced with Bordeaux, Rhône, and others.

lessons.3.slides.7.title: 💡 Professional Service Tips
lessons.3.slides.7.points.0: Communicate early: ask about preferences, budget, and restrictions
lessons.3.slides.7.points.1: Stay flexible: have alternatives ready (if a style doesn't appeal)
lessons.3.slides.7.points.2: Temperature control: whites at 10–12 °C, reds at 14–16 °C
lessons.3.slides.7.points.3: Decanting judgement: young wines benefit; old wines need care (they may be fragile)
lessons.3.slides.7.points.4: Portion control: 75–100 ml per pour to avoid over-intoxication
lessons.3.slides.7.points.5: Tell the story: a brief introduction adds experience value
lessons.3.slides.7.points.6: Watch the reaction: adjust subsequent pairings based on the guest's response
